title: Physical properties of aldehydes and ketones
keyIdea: Aldehydes and ketones have a polar C=O group, so permanent dipole–dipole forces act between their molecules as well as London forces. They have no H on O, so their molecules cannot hydrogen bond to each other. That puts their boiling points above alkanes and below alcohols of similar Mr. Small ones dissolve in water because water's δ+ H forms hydrogen bonds to lone pairs on the C=O oxygen. Longer chains raise the boiling point and lower solubility.

kid: Aldehydes and ketones both have a C=O group. Oxygen pulls the shared electrons harder than carbon does. So the O end is a little negative, δ−, and the C end is a little positive, δ+. The whole molecule has a dipole: one end is slightly plus and the other end is slightly minus.

Opposite ends of nearby molecules attract. These attractions are called permanent dipole–dipole forces. They add to the London forces that act between all molecules. So propanal, with Mr 58, boils at 48 °C. Butane, also Mr 58, has only London forces. It boils at about 0 °C.

But there is a limit. A hydrogen bond needs an H joined to N, O or F. In propanal and propanone every H is on carbon. So their molecules cannot hydrogen bond to each other. Propan-1-ol has an O–H group, so it does. It boils at 97 °C. The order is alkane, then carbonyl, then alcohol.

Water is different. Water has its own δ+ H atoms. They can reach the lone pairs on the C=O oxygen and form hydrogen bonds. That is why ethanal and propanone mix with water. A longer chain has more electrons, so it boils higher. But the long chain cannot bond with water, so it dissolves less.
adult: This is A-level chemistry, such as AQA 3.3.9 and OCR A module 6. It builds on the three forces between molecules: London forces, permanent dipole–dipole forces and hydrogen bonds. Learners compare boiling points with alkanes and alcohols of similar Mr. They also explain why short carbonyls mix with water.

The C=O bond is polar, so these molecules have a permanent dipole. No H is bonded to O, so they cannot hydrogen bond to each other. Butane boils at −0.5 °C, propanal at 48 °C and propan-1-ol at 97 °C. In water, lone pairs on the C=O oxygen accept hydrogen bonds from water's δ+ H. Up the series, London forces grow and the long chain cuts solubility.

Common mistakes: saying aldehydes hydrogen bond to each other because they contain oxygen; thinking boiling breaks the C=O bond; giving Mr as the reason propan-1-ol boils higher than propanal; drawing water's H bonded to the δ+ carbon; and saying longer chains dissolve less because they have weaker forces.

In the lab, learners rank compounds of matching Mr by boiling point and pick the forces between molecules. They draw a hydrogen bond from water to a C=O oxygen. They slide from C1 to C6 to see boiling point rise as solubility falls, then pin three compounds on a thermometer.

familyTip: Smell nail-polish remover (it is mostly propanone) and notice how fast a drop dries on a tile, then compare a drop of water. Talk about why the propanone escapes sooner: weaker forces between its molecules than water's hydrogen bonds.

visual.caption: Which forces act between molecules of each substance? Drag each card, or tap it and then tap a box.

lab.caption: Flagship lab: rank boiling points at matching Mr, name the forces, bond water to a C=O oxygen and slide along the aldehydes.

practice.prompt: Physical properties of aldehydes and ketones: why does propanal (Mr 58) boil higher than butane (Mr 58)?
choices: Its polar C=O adds permanent dipole–dipole forces
Propanal molecules hydrogen bond to each other
Its C=O bond must break when it boils
practice.hint: Both have similar London forces. What extra force does a polar C=O give?
practice.explain: The C=O bond is polar, so dipole–dipole forces act between propanal molecules as well as London forces. Butane has London forces only.

practice.prompt: An aldehyde has {n} carbon atoms, formula CnH2nO. What is its Mr? (C = 12, H = 1, O = 16)
practice.hint: Add 12 for each C, 1 for each of the 2n H atoms, and 16 for the O.
practice.explain: 12 × {n} + 2 × {n} + 16 = {=14*n+16}. Each CH2 unit adds 14, so Mr climbs by 14 per carbon.

practice.prompt: Which part of propanone accepts a hydrogen bond from a water molecule?
choices: A lone pair on the C=O oxygen
An H atom in a CH3 group
practice.hint: Water's H is δ+. It is attracted to a lone pair on an electronegative atom.
practice.explain: Water's δ+ H is attracted to a lone pair on the δ− oxygen. The carbonyl carbon is δ+ too, and the CH3 hydrogens have no lone pairs.

practice.prompt: An aldehyde has {n} carbon atoms, formula CnH2nO. How many electrons does one molecule have? (C has 6, H has 1, O has 8)
practice.hint: 6 for each C, 1 for each of the 2n H atoms, then 8 for the O.
practice.explain: 6 × {n} + 2 × {n} + 8 = {=8*n+8} electrons. More electrons means stronger London forces, so the boiling point rises along the series.

pool.prompt: Which forces act between molecules of propanone?
choices: London forces and permanent dipole–dipole forces
London forces, dipole–dipole forces and hydrogen bonds
pool.hint: Is the C=O polar? Is any H bonded to O?
pool.explain: The polar C=O gives dipole–dipole forces, and London forces act between all molecules. Every H is on carbon, so there are no hydrogen bonds between propanone molecules.

pool.prompt: Put these in order of boiling point, lowest first: propan-1-ol, butane, propanal.
pool.hint: Similar Mr. Rank by the strongest force between molecules.
pool.explain: Butane has London forces only (−0.5 °C), propanal adds dipole–dipole forces (48 °C), and propan-1-ol has hydrogen bonds (97 °C).

pool.prompt: Why is hexanal much less soluble in water than ethanal?
choices: Its long non-polar chain cannot hydrogen bond with water
pool.hint: Both have one C=O. What is different about the rest of the molecule?
pool.explain: Both can accept hydrogen bonds at the C=O oxygen, but the long hydrocarbon chain in hexanal cannot, so it breaks up water's hydrogen bonding and dissolves poorly.

pool.prompt: A ketone has {n} carbon atoms, formula CnH2nO. What is its Mr? (C = 12, H = 1, O = 16)
pool.hint: Ketones share the general formula CnH2nO with aldehydes.
pool.explain: 12 × {n} + 2 × {n} + 16 = {=14*n+16}. An aldehyde with the same carbons has the same Mr.

pool.prompt: When propanal boils, what is overcome?
pool.hint: Propanal vapour is still propanal molecules.
pool.explain: Boiling separates whole molecules. Covalent bonds inside each molecule, such as C=O, stay intact.

pool.prompt: Ethanal (Mr 44) boils at 20 °C. Ethanol (Mr 46) boils at 78 °C. What explains the gap?
choices: Ethanol has an O–H group, so it forms hydrogen bonds between molecules
pool.hint: The Mr values are almost the same. Look for an H bonded to O.
pool.explain: Ethanol's O–H lets its molecules hydrogen bond to each other. Ethanal has a dipole but no O–H, so its forces are weaker.

pool.prompt: Why do propanal molecules not form hydrogen bonds with each other?
choices: No hydrogen atom is bonded to the oxygen
pool.hint: A hydrogen bond needs an H on N, O or F as the donor.
pool.explain: Every H in propanal is bonded to carbon. The oxygen has lone pairs, so it can accept hydrogen bonds from water, but no propanal H can donate one.

pool.prompt: Going {k} steps up the aldehyde series adds {k} CH2 groups. How many extra electrons is that?
pool.hint: One CH2 has one C (6 electrons) and two H (1 each).
pool.explain: Each CH2 adds 6 + 1 + 1 = 8 electrons, so {k} steps add {=8*k}. London forces get stronger at each step.
